title: Escalation + Support SLA Policy Refresh — Product Ops Review Notes (contract language + tiering + GTM comms)
linked_artifacts: Jira: INT-333 (Jira automation: SLA reminders + required fields)
content:
Purpose
Capture Product Ops review notes on the Support SLA + escalation policy refresh before Confluence publication + Sales/CS enablement. Focus areas: (1) contract/SLA language safety, (2) tier definitions and naming, (3) how we communicate policy changes to Sales/CS without creating mismatched expectations vs Engineering SLOs/on-call practices.

Context / what is changing
Support leadership is standardizing severity language and creating tiered response/update targets across Hosted (self-serve), Dedicated, Private, and Enterprise variants. This is meant to reduce time-to-triage and to make escalation triggers predictable.

Important: these targets are “Support SLAs” (response + communication), not “Service availability/latency SLOs.” The new playbook must avoid implying additional service guarantees beyond what is in customer contracts.

Definitions and tiering (recommended to standardize in all docs + sales collateral)
We currently use terms inconsistently across teams (enterprise vs private vs dedicated). For this project, align to the following definitions:

1) Self-serve (Hosted API)
- Purchase motion: self-serve / PLG
- Typical terms: best-effort support, standard business-hours coverage (per published policy)
- Notes: avoid “SLA” wording externally unless we explicitly mean Support response targets (not uptime).

2) Dedicated
- Purchase motion: contract/commit for reserved capacity
- Support expectations: faster response/update cadence than self-serve; explicit escalation triggers for capacity events
- Important distinction: Dedicated does not automatically mean 24x7 incident comms unless contracted.

3) Private
- Deployment: customer VPC/on-prem package (regulated workloads)
- Support expectations: stronger coordination + runbook-driven troubleshooting; sensitive info handling requirements
- Important distinction: Private may have customer-operated components; avoid language that implies Redwood controls all failure domains.

4) Enterprise (commercial tier overlay)
- “Enterprise” is not a deployment mode; it is a commercial/support package that may apply to Hosted, Dedicated, or Private.
- Recommendation: In docs, use “Enterprise Support” as an overlay label (e.g., “Hosted + Enterprise Support”, “Dedicated + Enterprise Support”).
- If we keep “enterprise” as a row in SLA tables, we need a footnote that it is a support package (coverage/targets) and may require contract verification.

Contract / legal language considerations (Sofia review required)
High-risk phrasing to avoid (or to qualify clearly)
- “Guaranteed”, “commit”, “will”, “ensure”, “24/7”, “real-time”, “immediate” when describing response/mitigation.
- “Status page updates every X minutes” as a guarantee. Approval flows and incident classification can prevent that.
- “Credits” language that suggests automatic entitlements.

Safer phrasing patterns
- Use “target”, “aim”, “typical”, “during coverage hours”, “best-effort outside coverage hours unless contracted”.
- Separate: (A) first response targets, (B) update cadence targets while actively investigating, (C) escalation triggers (when we page Engineering/on-call).

Clarify “SLA” vs “SLO” vs “support targets”
- In internal docs, we can call the table “Support SLA targets” but should consistently qualify that this is about communication/response, not service performance guarantees.
- In customer-facing emails, prefer: “support response target” unless the customer’s MSA/SOW explicitly defines SLA response metrics.

Coverage hours and “after-hours” handling
- Must be consistent across: contracts, Zendesk/Jira automation, and what Support can actually staff.
- Recommendation: include a standard coverage statement at top of policy and avoid burying it in footnotes.
- For enterprise accounts with negotiated 24x7 support: require a visible “Contracted Coverage: Yes/No” field in CRM and/or Support ticket intake to avoid accidental over-promising.

Severity / priority terms (avoid mismatches)
- Support uses P0–P4; Engineering uses Sev0–Sev3.
- Product Ops recommendation: publish a single mapping table and include examples.
- Must clearly separate:
  - “Customer impact severity” (how bad)
  - “Engineering incident severity” (what it triggers operationally)
  - “Support ticket priority” (how we queue + respond)
- Risk: Sales/CS sometimes labels “P0” as “platform down” regardless of actual scope; this creates escalation churn and erodes trust. The new doc should emphasize objective triggers (error rate, # customers, region outage, revenue risk) rather than subjective urgency.

Credits / service remediation language
- Avoid any template language like “we will issue credits” or “credits are standard for X.”
- Recommended internal-only guidance:
  - Credits decisions are case-by-case per contract, impact evidence, and approvals.
  - Required approvals: CS leadership + Finance (and Legal if tied to contractual interpretation).
  - Support should never promise credits in initial acknowledgement.
- Provide an internal decision checklist (not to be copy/pasted to customers): incident duration, contract SLA clause applicability, customer’s documented impact, prior incidents, status page posts.

Status page / comms alignment
- We need to avoid turning the Support update cadence into a “status page update cadence.”
- Guidance:
  - Support/CS emails can follow a tighter cadence than status page updates.
  - Status page event qualification + approval flow remains separate.
  - If we promise “updates every 30 minutes,” clarify the channel: “via this email thread / ticket updates,” not status page.

Recommended policy structure (for Confluence + enablement)
1) One-page summary (internal)
- Coverage hours by tier/package
- First response target by tier
- Update cadence targets while active
- Escalation triggers + “when to page SRE”
- Link to escalation matrix + Slack bridge conventions

2) Customer-safe excerpt
- A short paragraph that Support/CS can reuse, with customer-safe wording.
- Avoid internal tool references (Jira fields, paging groups).

3) Contract verification note (internal)
- “If the customer requests a written statement of SLA terms, confirm their MSA/SOW. Do not quote the internal table as the contract.”

Communication plan: Sales + CS enablement
What Sales needs (practical)
- A 1-slide/1-pager: “What are Support response targets by package?” with clear footnotes.
- A talk track: how to position “Enterprise Support” vs “Dedicated/Private deployment.”
- A checklist of what to capture during sales cycles:
  - contracted coverage window
  - escalation contacts
  - required channels (email vs shared Slack)
  - compliance constraints (Private)

What CS needs (practical)
- A macro/snippet library aligned to the new policy:
  - acknowledgement message
  - mitigation update message
  - workaround message
  - “waiting on customer” language that pauses the update timer without sounding like we’re ignoring them
- A clear rule: CSMs should not create parallel escalation paths outside the playbook; they should route via Support + the bridge template.

Where to publish
- Internal: Confluence escalation playbook + Support process pages.
- External: only if/when we decide to publish a customer-facing support policy page; if not, keep customer-safe excerpt as a controlled template.

Operational / tooling implications (must be consistent or policy will fail)
- Jira automation must reflect the published targets:
  - SLA timers should measure first response and subsequent updates (where possible)
  - Required fields at intake: customer tier/package, region, model, request IDs
  - Clear “Paused – Waiting on Customer” state with rationale to prevent accidental SLA breach reporting
- CRM/source-of-truth for tier/package:
  - define which system wins (HubSpot vs internal billing) when mismatched
  - Support should have a single place to check “Enterprise Support: yes/no”

Open questions / risks to resolve before final publish
1) Naming: Do we keep “enterprise” as a tier in the SLA table?
- Recommendation: no; treat it as a support package overlay, or ensure every mention has a footnote.

2) Update cadence for enterprise accounts
- Product Ops view: do not hard-code “every 30 minutes” in a universal table unless we can staff it 24x7 for all enterprise customers.
- Alternative: publish a range and specify the tighter cadence is for active incidents within coverage hours.

3) After-hours policy
- Must be explicit. “Best effort” is acceptable only if defined (what constitutes best effort, who is on-call, and what triggers paging).

4) Private deployments (customer-operated components)
- Ensure wording makes clear what we can and cannot control.
- Include customer responsibilities for log collection / access if they run on-prem or control network policies.

5) Credits guidance visibility
- Keep credit decisioning internal-only; customer templates should route to CS for any credits discussion.

Action items (proposed owners)
- Sofia Mendes (Legal): review final wording for policy table + customer-safe excerpt; confirm no implied new contractual commitments.
- Rachel Kim (Enterprise CS): confirm enterprise package definitions and contracted coverage flags needed for CS workflows.
- Dev Patel (Support Ops): ensure Jira required fields + SLA timers align with the final policy; coordinate INT-333 changes.
- Sean Gallagher (SRE): confirm escalation triggers + paging thresholds align with on-call runbooks/SLO alerting.
- Elliot Price (Docs/DevEx): ensure Confluence page includes “contract verification” callout and avoids customer-sensitive examples.

Decision log (draft)
- Decision (recommended): Use “Support response targets” terminology in external/customer-safe templates; reserve “SLA” for internal policy and contract-specific discussions.
- Decision (recommended): Treat “Enterprise Support” as an overlay package, not a deployment tier.
- Pending: finalize update cadence language (hourly vs 30 min) and define how “waiting on customer” affects update cadence expectations.

Notes to self (Product Ops)
- Once this publishes, we should audit:
  - any sales collateral that mentions 24x7 support
  - CS onboarding/QBR decks that reference “SLA” loosely
  - status page messaging guidelines, to ensure Support doesn’t commit to status updates beyond incident policy
- Metrics to track post-rollout: first response SLA adherence by tier, incident bridge creation time, # of exec escalations triggered by “misunderstood SLA,” credit request volume, repeat ticket deflection from known-issues articles.
